briefing:
Day 29: Kaliningrad Phase 1 at 95% (1,284/1,350) — completion expected Day 30 dawn. UNSC Resolution 2742 endorses Framework 14-0-1 (Russia abstains). NATO alert downgrade to enhanced readiness expected Day 30. Tsikhanouskaya announces return to Minsk.

The compliance picture is now overwhelming. Russia has overdelivered on every metric. The Day 30 milestone — when warhead transport planning begins under IAEA — will mark the transition from the emergency implementation phase to the long-term compliance architecture.

UNSC 2742 gives the Framework the weight of international law. Russia's abstention (rather than veto) was negotiated as part of the sanctions relief provisions — a concession that costs Moscow nothing substantively but signals willingness to operate within the multilateral system.

Tsikhanouskaya's return to Minsk will be the most emotionally charged moment of the Belarusian transition. Her candidacy transforms the 90-day election from an abstract roadmap into a concrete democratic contest.

Markets: Oil $70, ruble 107/USD. Implementation Day 4 of 90. Phase 1 completion imminent.
narrative:
Day 29 brings Kaliningrad Phase 1 to within sight of completion. At 14:00 CET, the OSCE announces that 1,284 of 1,350 personnel have departed — 95% of Phase 1, with the remaining 66 (a logistics and base maintenance detachment) scheduled for departure at dawn on Day 30. The drawdown has been executed with military precision and complete transparency. In four days, Russia has accomplished what the Framework allowed seven days to complete.

The acceleration is not accidental. In Moscow, Kremlin insiders leak that Putin personally ordered the front-loaded timeline to create maximum leverage for the Day 30 warhead planning milestone. The logic is simple: if Russia overdelivers on Kaliningrad, it builds irresistible political momentum for the sanctions relief timeline. Sullivan, briefing the President at Mar-a-Lago, acknowledges the strategy: 'They're trying to create a compliance snowball effect. It's working.'

NATO Secretary General Rutte formally announces that upon completion of Kaliningrad Phase 1, the North Atlantic Council will convene to downgrade the alliance's alert level from Article 5 invoked to enhanced readiness. The downgrade is expected on Day 30 — exactly 30 days after Russia's armored columns first rolled through the Suwalki Gap. Rutte describes it as 'a measured response to verified compliance, not a declaration that all is well. NATO remains vigilant.'

In Belarus, the democratic transition gains tangible form. The transitional council publishes draft election regulations — OSCE-standard rules covering voter registration, campaign finance, media access, and international observation. Twenty-one political parties have now registered. Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya, who spent four years in Lithuanian exile after the disputed 2020 election, announces she will return to Minsk on Day 30 to formally register as a presidential candidate. The announcement electrifies Belarusian civil society.

The UN Security Council passes Resolution 2742, endorsing the Istanbul Framework Agreement. The vote is 14-0 with one abstention (Russia, which abstains rather than vetoes as a negotiated concession). China votes in favor. The resolution provides the Framework with the full weight of international law and establishes a monitoring mechanism through the Secretary-General's office.

surprises: At Minsk National Airport, something remarkable happens in preparation for Tsikhanouskaya's announced return. Maintenance workers, acting without orders from the transitional council, spend the evening painting over the last Lukashenko-era propaganda murals in the arrivals hall — replacing images of the former dictator with the white-red-white flag of democratic Belarus. Airport security guards, many of whom served under Lukashenko, make no move to stop them. By midnight, the transformation is complete. Social media images of the repainting go viral across Belarus with the hashtag #НовыйДзень (New Day). The transitional council, surprised but pleased, formally adopts the white-red-white flag as the interim state flag the following morning — the first time it has flown officially since 1995.
